title_idea: The Wudu Verse Assumes You WILL Pray — and Only 'Maybe' You'll Be Impure
reveal: The ablution verse uses two different Arabic 'if/when' words back to back. For prayer it uses idha ('when you rise to pray') — the particle Arabic reserves for something certain and expected to recur. For being in a state of major impurity, being ill, or travelling, it switches to in ('if you are junub... if you are ill... or on a journey') — the particle for something contingent that may or may not happen. So the grammar quietly assumes prayer is the settled rhythm of a believer's life (it is a 'when', not an 'if'), while treating impurity, sickness and travel as the exceptions that interrupt it. The default is worship; everything else is the deviation from it.
substrate: 5:6 — the prayer clause is governed by إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ (idha, the temporal particle for the certain/recurring). The very next clauses switch particle: وَإِن كُنتُمْ جُنُبًا ... وَإِن كُنتُم مَّرْضَىٰ أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ (in, the conditional particle for the hypothetical). Same verse, two distinct particles (LEM:إِذا vs LEM:إِن in the corpus), not interchangeable in classical Arabic.
grounding: The idha (definite/expected time) vs in (hypothetical, may-not-occur) distinction is standard classical nahw. Its application to this verse — prayer certain, impurity contingent — is noted by later mufassirun-grammarians (Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit; al-Alusi). The four sources pulled by cross_reference_tafsir.mjs (al-Tabari, al-Jalalayn, Ibn Kathir, al-Muyassar) treat the fiqh of wudu; al-Tabari records ikhtilaf over whether idha means 'every time you rise' or 'when you intend', which itself turns on the particle's force. RECOVERED GRAMMAR; the theological payoff ('worship is the assumed default') should be presented as a reflective reading, not a fiqh ruling.
overlap_note: No Ma'idah (Surah 5) tadabbur file exists on the site — the whole surah is currently uncovered. Not among the 185 published articles. Fresh.
imposed_check: The two particles are literally different words (idha vs in) inside the same ayah — a lexical fact of the mushaf text, not an interpretive overlay; only the significance is interpretive.
angle: Everyone has washed for prayer a thousand times. Almost no one notices the verse is grammatically built on the assumption that you WILL pray — prayer is the 'when', impurity is the 'if'.

title_idea: Fear Before Hunger, or Hunger Before Fear? The Order Flips Depending on Whether God Is Testing You or Punishing You
reveal: Two verses pair the exact same two hardships — fear and hunger — but in opposite order. When God describes TESTING the believers (2:155), He lists fear first, then hunger. When He describes PUNISHING an ungrateful town that had lived in ample provision (16:112), He lists hunger first, then fear. The order is not decorative: a test of faith opens with the inner, psychological trial (fear); a punishment for ingratitude about provision strikes first at the very blessing they were ungrateful for (hunger), then fear. Same two words, reversed — and the reversal tracks whether you are being refined or being judged.
substrate: 2:155 وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَيْءٍ مِّنَ الْخَوْفِ وَالْجُوعِ — khawf (fear, root خ-و-ف) BEFORE ju' (hunger, root ج-و-ع); context is bala' (a test of believers). 16:112 فَأَذَاقَهَا اللَّهُ لِبَاسَ الْجُوعِ وَالْخَوْفِ — ju' (hunger) BEFORE khawf (fear); context is a town that was amina (secure) with rizq raghad (abundant provision from every place) that denied God's favors and was punished. Both orders confirmed in the Uthmani text.
grounding: The context of 16:112 (ample provision -> ingratitude about that provision -> hunger) is explicit in al-Tabari and al-Muyassar (both pulled). The cross-verse observation that the ORDER itself tracks test-vs-punishment is the reading of later mufassirun/balaghiyyin (al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb; al-Alusi); the pulled basic sources supply the context but do not make the explicit cross-comparison — so present the order-payoff as recovered balagha offered as reflection, resting on the context the classical sources DO state.
overlap_note: The Baqarah 2:153-157 tadabbur file spotlights the partitive bi-shay'in min ('SOMETHING of fear', a portion) — a different grammatical point. The Nahl 16:112-119 file spotlights the 'garment' (libas) metaphor of hunger and fear. Neither file notes the fear/hunger ORDER, and neither cross-references the other verse. Fresh contrast.
imposed_check: The word order in each verse is a fixed textual fact, and the two verses genuinely pair the identical two roots (خ-و-ف and ج-و-ع) in opposite sequence — nothing is projected; only the significance of the reversal is interpretive.
angle: You would never notice that two far-apart verses use the same pair of words backwards — until you see the order itself is telling you whether God is testing you or punishing you.

title_idea: The Grammar Stops Calling You 'You' the Moment the Sea Turns Calm
reveal: One sailing-verse begins by speaking straight TO you: 'He is the One who carries YOU on land and sea... until when YOU are in the ships.' Then, at the exact moment a good wind blows and the passengers relax, the grammar suddenly stops addressing them as 'you' and switches to 'them' — 'and the ships sailed with THEM... and THEY rejoiced in it.' God turns away from face-to-face address and describes them from a distance, as if to a third party. Then the storm hits — and they cry out 'if YOU save US' — snapping the address back to the second person. The pronoun shifts map the relationship: intimate 'you' while in God's care, drifting to distant 'them' the instant comfort makes them forget Him, back to desperate 'You' the moment they are terrified.
substrate: 10:22 — opens 2nd person plural: يُسَيِّرُكُمْ (-kum) ... حَتَّىٰ إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي الْفُلْكِ (kuntum, 2MP). Shifts to 3rd person plural: وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم (bihim, 3MP) ... وَفَرِحُوا بِهَا (fariḥu, 3MP) ... وَجَاءَهُمُ الْمَوْجُ. In the storm the direct address returns: دَعَوُا اللَّهَ ... لَئِنْ أَنجَيْتَنَا (anjayta-na, 2MS verb + 'us'). Person values are encoded in the segment features (2MP kum/kuntum vs 3MP hum/waw suffixes vs the -ta of anjayta).
grounding: This verse is the classic textbook example of iltifat — the rhetorical turn from address (khitab) to absence (ghayba). Al-Zamakhshari cites 10:22 in al-Kashshaf precisely for this turn; al-Razi discusses it in Mafatih al-Ghayb. RECOVERED BALAGHA (named source).
overlap_note: The Yunus 10:21-24 tadabbur file treats the psychological rhythm ('tasted mercy -> scheming -> rescue -> outrage') and the verb adhaqna, but does NOT spotlight the you->them->you person-shift itself. Not in the published articles. Fresh angle on an otherwise-covered verse.
imposed_check: The pronoun persons are carried by the words themselves (kum vs hum vs the -ta suffix of anjayta) — mechanically readable in the corpus features, not read into the text.
angle: The verse literally changes how God is talking to you at the precise second you stop thinking about Him — and you can watch it happen in the pronouns, then reverse when the storm arrives.

title_idea: They Said God's Hand Is Chained. He Answered With Two.
reveal: A group mocked that 'God's hand is chained' — using the SINGULAR, one shackled hand, an image of stinginess. The reply does three things with grammatical number in a single breath. First it turns their own image back on them in the PLURAL: 'may THEIR hands be chained.' Then, instead of a matching singular, it answers with the DUAL: 'rather, both His hands are outstretched.' They shrank God to one bound hand; the reply widens Him to two open ones. The number itself is the rebuttal — you pictured restriction (one, chained); the answer is doubled, unbound giving.
substrate: 5:64 — يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ: yad is feminine SINGULAR (features FS), 'hand', chained (their claim). غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ: aydihim is PLURAL (features FP), 'their hands' chained — turned back on them. بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ: yadahu is DUAL (features FD), 'His two hands' outstretched — the answer. Three distinct grammatical numbers on the same root ي-د-ي (singular / plural / dual), all confirmed in the corpus features.
grounding: al-Muyassar (pulled) glosses yadahu mabsutatan as boundless giving — He is al-Jawwad al-Karim, nothing restrains His spending. Classical balaghiyyin (al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari) read the dual as intensifying generosity against the singular-chained claim. RECOVERED. Note for the writer: 'hand' here is a divine attribute handled per classical adab (bila kayf / affirm-without-anthropomorphizing) — the reveal is strictly about the grammatical NUMBER move, not the attribute debate.
overlap_note: Surah al-Ma'idah has no tadabbur file on the site (the whole surah is uncovered). Not among the published articles. Fresh.
imposed_check: Singular, dual and plural are grammatically marked on the three surface words (يَد / أَيْدِي / يَدَا) — this is morphology present in the text, fully checkable, not an inference.
angle: The comeback is not merely 'no, God is generous' — the Arabic literally out-numbers the insult: one chained hand answered by two open ones, with their own plural hands chained in between.

title_idea: The Quran Names the Woman First for Adultery, the Man First for Theft — and the Order Is the Argument
reveal: Two punishment-verses each list a male and a female offender. In adultery (24:2) the woman is named first: 'the adulteress and the adulterer.' In theft (5:38) the man is named first: 'the thief [m.] and the thief [f.].' Standard Arabic default puts the masculine first, so BOTH orderings are deliberate — and they flip by crime. Classical readers explain the flip by where each offense is anchored. Read as a pair, the verses show the Quran ordering the two parties by the internal logic of each specific sin, not by any fixed gender ranking.
substrate: 24:2 الزَّانِيَةُ وَالزَّانِي — feminine zaniyah (ACT_PCPL, F) BEFORE masculine zani (ACT_PCPL, M). 5:38 وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ — masculine sariq (ACT_PCPL, M) BEFORE feminine sariqah (ACT_PCPL, F). Segment order confirmed in both; the masculine-first default is broken only in 24:2.
grounding: The fronting-flip and its reasons are discussed explicitly by al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf), al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb), and al-Qurtubi. IMPORTANT: the four sources pulled by cross_reference_tafsir.mjs (Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari, al-Muyassar, al-Jalalayn) treat the hadd RULINGS, not the ordering — so the ordering-explanation must be verified in al-Kashshaf / Mafatih before publishing. Sensitive topic: frame with ikhtilaf, and do NOT let it imply a 'women are worse' ranking (the classical explanations are about the locus/initiative of the act, not moral hierarchy).
overlap_note: HEAVY PARTIAL OVERLAP — the site's An-Nur 24:2 tadabbur file (ayah-002.md) already publishes 'the woman is named first, breaking the masculine-first default' as its central reveal. This candidate is ONLY viable if built on the CONTRAST with theft (5:38, man first), which neither the An-Nur file nor any Ma'idah file covers (Ma'idah is uncovered). If the editorial team judges the contrast too close to the existing 24:2 piece, DROP it. Flagged, lower-confidence.
imposed_check: The ordering is a bare textual fact in both verses; only the explanation of WHY the order flips is interpretive, and classical vs modern readings must be marked as such.
angle: One crime names the woman first, another names the man first — evidence that the Quran's word order is not habit but argument. (High adversarial-quotation sensitivity; needs careful framing.)

title_idea: The Quran Never Tells You What Yusuf Looked Like — It Shows You the Cut Hands Instead
reveal: The women of the city are each handed a knife and some fruit; Yusuf is told to walk out among them. The verse never describes his face, never uses a word for 'beautiful,' never gives a single feature. Instead it deletes the description entirely and gives you only the effect: they were so overcome that they cut their own hands without noticing, and gasped 'this is no mortal — this is a noble angel.' The omission IS the portrait. By refusing to describe him and showing only the wound, the verse makes his beauty something you infer from the reaction — more overwhelming than any adjective could have delivered.
substrate: 12:31 — فَلَمَّا رَأَيْنَهُ أَكْبَرْنَهُ وَقَطَّعْنَ أَيْدِيَهُنَّ ('when they saw him, they deemed him overwhelming, and cut their hands'). No adjective or noun describing Yusuf's appearance occurs anywhere in the verse; it carries only the verb akbarnahu ('they deemed him great/overwhelming') and the physical reaction. The described object — his beauty — is grammatically ABSENT (hadhf / ijaz: the thing that would be described is omitted, and the response substitutes for it).
grounding: The mufassirun read his beauty FROM the reaction: al-Muyassar (pulled) — 'his beauty was unlike any known among humans,' inferred from the self-wounding; al-Tabari similarly narrates the astonishment. The framing of the OMISSION itself as a deliberate rhetorical technique (show-don't-tell / bulugh by ellipsis) is a LITERARY reading — flag as modern/reflective, though it rests on the classical inference-from-effect. Also widely repeated in popular du'at discourse, so not novel-sounding; not a claimed balagha attribution.
overlap_note: The Yusuf 12:30-35 tadabbur file (ayahs-030-035.md) covers the scene (the plot of the women, Yusuf clinging to protection) but does NOT spotlight the omission-of-description. Fresh angle, but adjacent to well-known preaching. Mark clearly as literary observation.
imposed_check: It is verifiable that the verse contains NO descriptive word for Yusuf's appearance — the substrate is an ABSENCE, checkable by reading every word of 12:31; the response (cut hands, akbarnahu) is what the text supplies in its place.
angle: The most famous beauty in scripture, and the text flatly refuses to describe it — you are made to feel it through ten cut hands instead.
